description: Explore the cutting-edge physical tools scientists use to measure the heat, light, and mechanical forces of individual molecules in real-time.

slides.title: Welcome to Biological Spectroscopy
slides.content:
# Measuring the Invisible

Welcome to **Biological Spectroscopy and Techniques**!

We know what proteins look like (Structure) and how they should move in a computer (Dynamics). But how do we physically measure their energy, folding, and movement in the real world?

## What You Will Learn:
- **Spectroscopic Methods** - Using light to see shape
- **Calorimetric Techniques** - Measuring the heat of biology
- **Microscopy Advances** - Breaking the limit of light
- **Single Molecule Techniques** - Playing tug-of-war with DNA

Let's head into the laboratory.

slides.title: Spectroscopic Methods
slides.content:
# Using Light to See Shape

**Spectroscopy** is the study of how matter interacts with electromagnetic radiation (light).

If you shine a specific wavelength of light through a tube of dissolved protein, the protein will absorb some of that light. By measuring exactly which colors (wavelengths) are absorbed, we can deduce what the protein is made of, and even how it is folded!

slides.title: Circular Dichroism
slides.content:
# Circular Dichroism (CD)

The most common spectroscopic tool for biophysicists is **Circular Dichroism (CD)**.

It uses polarized light (light that spins like a corkscrew). 
- Because proteins are "chiral" (they have a left-handed or right-handed twist), they absorb left-spinning light differently than right-spinning light.
- By measuring this difference, a CD machine can instantly tell you if your protein is mostly folded into Alpha-Helices, Beta-Sheets, or if it is just a random, unfolded mess!
- It doesn't give you a perfect 3D picture, but it is incredibly fast and cheap for checking if your protein is folded correctly.

slides.title: Spectroscopy Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of using light.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the primary use of Circular Dichroism (CD) spectroscopy in a biophysics lab?
quizOptions: To instantly kill all bacteria in a water sample
To determine if a protein in solution is properly folded into secondary structures (like Alpha-Helices)
To take a perfect, high-resolution 3D photograph of an atom
To measure the weight of a DNA molecule

slides.title: Calorimetric Techniques
slides.content:
# Measuring Biological Heat

Whenever a drug binds to a protein, or a protein folds into its 3D shape, tiny amounts of chemical energy are released as Heat (exothermic) or absorbed as Cold (endothermic).

**Calorimetry** is the science of measuring these incredibly tiny temperature changes.

slides.title: ITC and DSC
slides.content:
# The Two Thermometers

## Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC)
Used to measure Binding. 
You put a protein in a tiny cup. You slowly drip a drug into the cup. As the drug binds to the protein, it releases a microscopic pulse of heat. The ITC machine measures this heat spike, telling you EXACTLY how tightly the drug binds to the protein!

## Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC)
Used to measure Stability. 
You slowly heat up a protein until it "melts" (unfolds). The DSC machine measures exactly how much heat energy it takes to force the protein to unfold, telling you exactly how stable the molecular machine is.

slides.title: Calorimetry Quiz
slides.quizQuestion: If a pharmaceutical company wants to know exactly how tightly their new drug physically binds to a target protein, which technique would they use to measure the microscopic heat released during binding?

slides.title: Microscopy Advances
slides.content:
# Breaking the Limit of Light

For a hundred years, physics dictated that you could not see anything smaller than half the wavelength of visible light (about 200 nanometers). Proteins are 5 nanometers. They were "invisible."

In 2014, the Nobel Prize was awarded for **Super-Resolution Microscopy**, which broke this physical limit using clever tricks with fluorescent glowing dyes, allowing us to see individual proteins moving inside a living cell!

slides.title: FRET
slides.content:
# FRET: The Molecular Ruler

How do we know if two proteins actually touch each other inside a living cell?
We use **FRET (Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer)**.

1. You attach a Blue glowing dye to Protein A, and a Green glowing dye to Protein B.
2. You shine a light that ONLY makes the Blue dye glow.
3. If Protein A and Protein B are far apart, you see Blue light.
4. BUT, if they physically touch each other, the energy from the Blue dye instantly jumps over to the Green dye. Suddenly, the cell glows Green!

FRET acts as a microscopic ruler to prove that two machines are interacting!

slides.title: Single Molecule Techniques
slides.content:
# Playing with Single Molecules

Traditionally, science measures a beaker containing a billion proteins and takes the average. 
But modern biophysics allows us to grab and manipulate ONE SINGLE MOLECULE at a time.

slides.title: Optical Tweezers
slides.content:
# Optical Tweezers

This sounds like science fiction, but it is real (and won a Nobel Prize in 2018).

An **Optical Tweezer** uses a highly focused laser beam to physically trap and hold a microscopic plastic bead. 
- Scientists attach one end of a DNA molecule to the glass slide, and the other end to the floating bead.
- By moving the laser beam, they can physically stretch the single DNA molecule like a rubber band!
- They can measure exactly how much force it takes to rip the DNA apart, or watch a single motor protein crawl along the DNA and measure its individual "footsteps"!

slides.title: Atomic Force Microscopy
slides.content:
# Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM)

Instead of using light to see a protein, what if you just touch it?

**AFM** uses a microscopic needle (like the needle on an old record player) that is literally one atom thick at the tip.
- The needle is dragged across the surface of a cell membrane.
- As the needle bumps over individual proteins sticking out of the membrane, a laser measures how the needle bounces.
- A computer translates the bounces into a perfect 3D topological map of the surface, allowing you to "feel" the shape of individual molecules!

slides.title: Single Molecule Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of the cutting edge.
slides.quizQuestion: How does an 'Optical Tweezer' allow a scientist to physically stretch a single DNA molecule?
quizOptions: By using microscopic metal pliers controlled by a robot
By freezing the DNA in ice and cracking it
By using a highly focused laser beam to trap and pull a microscopic bead attached to the end of the DNA
By using a massive electromagnet to pull the DNA

slides.title: Summary of Spectroscopy
slides.content:
# Biophysics Techniques Summary

## Key Takeaways:

### Light and Heat
- **Circular Dichroism (CD)** uses polarized light to check if a protein is folded correctly.
- **Calorimetry (ITC and DSC)** measures the microscopic heat released when drugs bind or proteins unfold.

### The Cutting Edge
- **FRET** uses jumping fluorescent energy to prove when two proteins physically touch inside a cell.
- **Optical Tweezers** use lasers to physically stretch single DNA molecules.
- **AFM** uses a one-atom-thick needle to physically 'feel' the shape of molecules on a surface.

> **Congratulations!** You have completed the entire Advanced Science Curriculum! You now understand the physics of life.
